Intercessory prayer

Worship and practice · Prayer

Intercessory prayer

5 sectionsNot completed
Notes

Intercession means prayer for other people. St. Cassian distinguishes it from other kinds of prayer, while the published service excerpt gives language associated with consolation and affliction.[1][2]

What kinds of prayer does St. Cassian distinguish?[1]

St. Cassian begins with the apostolic list of supplications, prayers, intercessions and thanksgivings. He treats these as terms requiring explanation rather than assuming they all mean exactly the same thing. The passage introduces the question of how these forms of prayer are related.[1]

Read original passage

Four kinds of prayer

And therefore, when we have laid this down with regard to the character of prayer, although not so fully as the importance of the subject requires, but as fully as the exigencies of time permit, and at any rate as our slender abilities admit, and our dulness of heart enables us,--a still greater difficulty now awaits us; viz., to expound one by one the different kinds of prayer, which the Apostle divides in a fourfold manner, when he says as follows: "I exhort therefore first of all that supplications, prayers, intercessions, thanksgivings be made." [1593] And we cannot possibly doubt that this division was not idly made by the Apostle. And to begin with we must investigate what is meant by supplication, by prayer, by intercession, and by thanksgiving. Next we must inquire whether these four kinds are to be taken in hand by him who prays all at once, i.e., are they all to be joined together in every prayer,--or whether they are to be offered up in turns and one by one, as, for instance, ought at one time supplications, at another prayers, at another intercessions, and at another thanksgivings to be offered, or should one man present to God supplications, another prayers, another intercessions, another thanksgivings, in accordance with that measure of age, to which each soul is advancing by earnestness of purpose?

What is intercession directed toward?[1]

St. Cassian describes intercession as prayer for others, including loved ones, rulers and the peace of the whole world. Its scope therefore extends beyond a person’s own immediate needs. This is the particular meaning supplied by the quoted explanation.[1]

Read original passage

Intercessions

In the third place stand intercessions, which we are wont to offer up for others also, while we are filled with fervour of spirit, making request either for those dear to us or for the peace of the whole world, and to use the Apostle's own phrase, we pray "for all men, for kings and all that are in authority." [1597]

How does the hymn express prayer in affliction?[2]

The Third Hour hymn addresses Christ in a condition of sorrow and asks for consolation and his sustaining presence. Its language places affliction within an appeal to Christ and praise of the Holy Spirit. The source is an existing service hymn, not an original prayer written for this lesson.[2]

Read original passage

Third Hour collect-hymn

Grant speedy and steadfast consolation unto thy servants, O Jesus, when our spirit is cast down within us. Depart not from our souls in affliction; be not far from our thoughts in time of trouble; but always defend us. Draw near unto us, draw near unto us, thou who art omnipresent! As thou art ever with thine Apostles, so, also, O Bountiful One, unite thyself unto those who long for thee; that with one accord we may sing praises unto thee, and laud thy most holy Spirit.

Intercession in an OCA resource[3]

The linked OCA article concerns intercessory prayer. It accompanies St. Cassian’s explanation of prayer offered for other people.[3]
